title: Vessantara gives
hook: the generous prince gives away the kingdom's rain-bringing white elephant and is exiled

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ruru deer, who saved the man who sold him out, and then saved him again. Your line was do it anyway. Did someone get a kindness they'll never notice? Day ninety-two, and the last and longest Jataka begins.

Think of the easiest thing you gave away this year. A bag of old clothes, maybe. Things you'd stopped wanting anyway. Now think of something you'd find hard to give. The good jacket. A free Saturday. The last of something. That's a different feeling, isn't it? Today we start the most famous story in the Theravada Buddhist world. It's the last of the five hundred and forty-seven Jatakas in the Pali collection, and by far the longest. In Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Sri Lanka, people know it the way others know a great national epic. It's about a prince who gives away the thing nobody wanted him to give.
screen: `THE BAG OF OLD CLOTHES.` → `THE THING YOU'D RATHER KEEP.` → `THE LAST AND LONGEST JATAKA.`

segments.voice: Vessantara is the crown prince of the Sivi kingdom, and from childhood he loves to give. The story says he wanted to give even his own heart or eyes if someone asked. His kingdom owns a treasure: a magnificent white elephant, and wherever it goes, the rain comes. Then envoys arrive from a neighboring land, Kalinga, where the rains have failed and the fields are cracking. They ask for the elephant. And Vessantara, sitting on its back, pours water over their hands, the old sign of a gift, and gives it to them. Picture the city the next morning. Their rain has just walked out of the gate. The people are furious, and they demand his exile. His father, the king, gives in. So Vessantara leaves the palace for a mountain in the forest, and his wife Maddi and their two small children choose to go with him. On the way out, he gives away even more: his chariot, his horses, walking the last part on foot with his children in their arms. Why is this the story Buddhists put last? Because Vessantara is the Buddha's final human birth before the one in which he awakens, and in this life he completes the perfection of giving, dana. It isn't told as a sensible budget. It's told as giving taken as far as it can go. And the story doesn't hide the cost. A whole city is angry. A family loses its home. Tomorrow, the cost gets harder still. Today just notice the carry: the gift you feel is usually the one that costs something.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT THAT BRINGS THE RAIN.` · `GIVEN TO A LAND IN DROUGHT.` · `THE CITY DEMANDS HIS EXILE.` · `THE PERFECTION OF GIVING.` · then, large: `GENEROSITY COSTS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Now think of one thing you have that you'd rather keep: an object, an hour, some attention. Hold it in your mind. Notice where the reluctance sits in your body. The chest, the hands, the jaw. You don't have to give it away yet. Just breathe with the pull between keeping and giving, and let both be there. Then, gently, picture the moment of handing it over, water poured over open hands. See what happens in the body. The bell holds the time.
Vessantara gives. The prince who gave the rain-bringing elephant, and was sent into exile for it.
Your line: generosity costs. Today, give one thing you'd rather keep. Something small, but something you'll feel. Day ninety-two.

howItsDone: In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia the Vessantara story is recited in full at a yearly temple festival, often in a single day, and Buddhists across the Theravada world treat it as the great story of dana, generosity.

fork.setup: you're the prince. envoys from a land in drought ask for your kingdom's rain-bringing elephant. what do you do?
options: refuse: your own people need the rain.
fork.reveal: he pours water over their hands and gives it. it costs him the palace: the city demands his exile.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, generosity; Vessantara is said to complete the perfection of dana.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prince who was bad with money.
what it means: the perfection of giving, taken as far as it can go, with the cost told plainly.
what a scholar hears: Jataka 547 is the last of the ten long 'great births'; it's recited at the Thai Thet Mahachat festival and painted on temple walls across Southeast Asia.
